sections.title: What You Have To Do
sections.content: Spanish has two ways of saying must, and the difference is who it applies to. 'Tengo que' is personal — I have to, and the verb changes with the person: tengo que, tienes que, tiene que. 'Hay que' is the rule for everyone, and never changes at all: hay que trabajar en equipo. Both are followed by a plain infinitive.

sections.title: tener que — one person has to
hay que — everyone has to
rows: you have to work as a team
hay que ayudar a los compañeros
you have to help your colleagues

items.spanish: Se levanta temprano porque tiene que llegar antes de las ocho.
items.english: He gets up early because he has to be there before eight.

items.spanish: Hay que trabajar en equipo y hay que ayudar a los compañeros.
items.english: You have to work as a team and help your colleagues.

items.spanish: Tengo que aprender muchas cosas, pero todos son muy amables.
items.english: I have to learn a lot, but everyone is very kind.

items.spanish: Hay que descansar después de un día largo.
items.english: You need to rest after a long day.

sections.content: 'Hay que' has no subject at all — it is the same 'hay' you have used since Lesson 4, so there is no 'hay que yo' and no plural. If you want to name who must do it, you need 'tener que'.
